<reason>B built the debate's decision frame — the slogan-or-Ajaokuta dilemma anchored in the word "over" — and sustained it through every speech. A answered the slogan horn honestly with concrete marginal trade-offs (export duties, megawatt allocation, rail capital), a genuine strength, and A's Botswana flip was the best single move of the debate. But B met the teeth with concrete, unrebutted costs (farmgate prices, cocoa smuggling, taxing the FX earner), gave the historically more accurate account of Korea's learning-stage exports to rich distant consumers, and A never answered B's Q2 — no country named that industrialized selling mainly to equally poor neighbors. A's closing sidestepped the smuggling/farmgate mechanism and answered the purchasing-power gap only by asserting the market "must be built," which B's final speech directly dismantled ("a market you must build is a market you do not have on the day the megawatt moves"). B's clipped Rebuttal 2 is a small execution cost but the argument was substantively complete. A was more rhetorically elegant; B was more decisively responsive.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 2: absorbing A's "teeth" by endorsing the win-win instruments while showing the hard instruments tax farmers and the treasury to fund factories that cannot yet compete, then converting A's Korea history into the concession that the rich world — not poor neighbors — was the ramp, leaving A's precedent burden unanswered through the end.</best_rebuttal>
